framework: 1. Admit the mind keeps running. 2. Notice when it turns inward and when it runs out. 3. Change the setting if you must. 4. Reason it through: 'I am not this thought.' 5. Return, as many times as it takes.
modern_parallels: I sit to meditate and within ten seconds I am planning my day.
Every app says ten minutes of calm and I cannot do one.
At night my mind jumps between work, money and family and will not stop.
I want peace so badly that the wanting itself makes me restless.

key_verses.sanskrit: उद्दालको नाम मुनिर्मौनी मानी महामतिः । अप्राप्तयौवनः पूर्वमुवासोद्दामतापसः ॥
key_verses.gist: There was a silent sage named Uddalaka, proud and of great mind, young and given to austerity.

key_verses.sanskrit: विषयैर्नीयमाने तु चित्ते मर्कटचञ्चले । न स लेभे समाधानप्रतिष्ठां प्रीतिदायिनीम् ॥
key_verses.gist: His mind, restless as a monkey, was dragged by objects, and he could not find the settled calm that gives joy.

content_hook: A young sage sat down to meditate and his mind ran off within moments. He kept failing for a long time. Then he tried something different.

title: Vitahavya closes his eyes in a cave and finds his mind still talking
the_moment: The sage Vitahavya gives up his rituals and goes to a cave in the Vindhyas to sit still. He shuts his eyes and draws in his senses. His mind keeps going, jumping 'from pot to cloth to cart' like a leaf on the waves.
what_they_did: He talks to his senses and then to his mind directly, as one would to a restless friend: you are only passages, you have no light of your own; mind, you are borrowing your life from awareness and calling it 'I'.
the_turn: He sees that the mind has no light of its own; awareness is what knows it. Once that is clear, the mind loses its hold.
outcome: He sits in samadhi for a very long time; when he returns, he lives free, and Vasishtha holds him up as a model.
whole_arc_note: The long burial of his body in mud during samadhi is part of the later story and is not a practice to imitate. The usable core is the self-talk: a calm, reasoning dialogue with one's own mind.
teaching: The mind runs because it borrows life from awareness; seeing that, one stops obeying it.
framework: 1. Sit and close the senses. 2. Notice the mind still moving. 3. Speak to it plainly. 4. Ask what knows the mind. 5. Rest as that.
modern_parallels: I lie in bed with my eyes shut and my mind keeps talking.
Even on holiday, away from everything, my head is full of noise.
I argue with my own thoughts all night.
I removed every distraction and found the distraction was me.

key_verses.sanskrit: अहो नु चञ्चलमिदं प्रत्याहृतमपि क्षणात् । न मनः स्थैर्यमायाति तरङ्गप्रौढपर्णवत् ॥
key_verses.gist: How is it that though I have shut my outer organs, I cannot by any force stop my mind, which flutters like a leaf on the waves?

content_hook: He went to a cave, shut his eyes, blocked every sense. His mind kept talking. So he started talking back.

title: King Suraghu cannot bear to punish, and cannot afford not to
the_moment: Suraghu is a strong, fair king who rewards and punishes as his people deserve. But each punishment stays with him. 'Why do I crush the hearts of my people like sesame seeds in a press? They all feel pain.' He decides to stop, then sees that if he spares the wrongdoers, the good will be destroyed.
dilemma: Punishing hurts people he cares for; not punishing lets the strong destroy the weak.
what_they_did: When the sage Mandavya visits, Suraghu tells him plainly that this doubt is tearing at him 'like a lion's claws'. Mandavya does not tell him to stop governing. He tells him that such doubts melt by his own inquiry, and gives him a way to look into his mind.
the_turn: Alone, Suraghu examines himself and sees that pleasure and pain arise in the mind; he can act from evenness rather than from the sting of each decision.
outcome: He goes on ruling, rewarding and punishing, without inner torment. Later his old friend Parigha meets him and finds him at peace.
whole_arc_note: He keeps his duty, including punishment. The teaching is about the inner state of the one who must decide, not a licence for harshness or a call to resign. Keep both halves of the dilemma he states.
teaching: A ruler who must cause pain can act justly without being torn, by seeing that pain and pleasure arise in the mind and resting in the self.
framework: 1. State both sides of the bind honestly. 2. Take it to someone wise. 3. Look inward until the decision and the sting separate. 4. Keep doing the duty, evenly.
modern_parallels: I have to let three people go next week and I cannot sleep.
As a manager I hate giving bad reviews, but if I do not, the good people leave.
Disciplining my child makes me feel cruel, and not disciplining makes me feel weak.
I am a judge in a small way at work and every decision eats me up.

key_verses.sanskrit: हा कष्टमेव निग्राह्यो नित्यानुग्राह्य एष मे । दिष्ट्याद्य सुखवानस्मि कष्टमद्यास्मि दुःखवान् ॥
key_verses.gist: Alas, the pain of it: this one must be restrained, that one always favoured; today I am happy, today I suffer.

key_verses.sanskrit: महतां संगमेनार्तिः कस्य नाम न नश्यति । संदेहं तु परामार्तिमाहुरार्तिविदो जनाः ॥
key_verses.gist: Whose pain does not vanish in the company of the great? Those who know pain say doubt is the greatest pain.

content_hook: A king who had to punish people could not sleep over it. Stop punishing, and the good get crushed. A sage gave him a third way.

title: Two childhood friends meet in old age and admit they never found peace
the_moment: Bhasa and Vilasa grow up together in a hermitage on the Sahya mountain, 'one mind in two bodies'. After their parents die they go separate ways and spend long years in hard austerities. They meet again when both are old and worn, like two dry trees in a valley.
what_they_did: Vilasa greets his friend with great love and asks how the years went, and whether his austerities bore fruit. Bhasa answers honestly: how can we have rest while the passions are not subdued and the one thing worth knowing is not known? Our days pass in efforts that lead nowhere.
the_turn: The honest admission between friends: 'Life wastes away in trifling acts begun for wrong ends and petty hopes.' From it the two turn to inquiry together.
outcome: Vasishtha says they then attained understanding; the story is told to show that years of effort without discernment do not bring peace.
whole_arc_note: This is a tender story of friendship as well as of wasted effort. Keep the warmth of their meeting; the regret is shared, not one judging the other.
teaching: Years of effort without discernment wear out the body without bringing peace; only knowing the self brings rest.
modern_parallels: I met my school friend after thirty years and we both admitted we are not happy.
I worked so hard for decades and I do not know what it was for.
Retired now, and the peace I was promised never came.
I want one honest conversation with an old friend about what we did with our lives.

key_verses.sanskrit: अप्राप्तविमलज्ञानौ चिराज्जर्जरतापसौ । तावेकदा संघटिताविदमन्योन्यमूचतुः ॥
key_verses.gist: Long worn by austerity without attaining clear knowledge, the two met one day and spoke to each other.

key_verses.sanskrit: अयथार्थक्रियारम्भैः कदाशावेशपल्लवैः । क्षीयते कर्मभिस्तुच्छैरायुराहतकर्मभिः ॥
key_verses.gist: Life wastes away in acts begun for wrong ends, leafing out with petty hopes.

content_hook: Two best friends separated as boys and met again as old men. The first honest thing one said to the other was: I never found it.

title: King Janaka overhears a song in his garden, climbs to his roof alone, and questions everything
the_moment: Janaka is walking in his spring garden, prosperous and content. From a grove of tamala trees he hears unseen sages singing about the self that is neither the seer nor the seen. The song unsettles him completely.
what_they_did: He walks home in silence, sends his household away, and climbs alone to the highest terrace. Watching birds fly in every direction, he sees people hurrying the same way and questions his whole life: 'The days and nights pass and give me no chance to see what does not perish.' He resolves to string his scattered mind on the needle of reason.
the_turn: He finds the answer within by his own inquiry, without a teacher in front of him. Then, when his attendants come to remind him of the day's duties, he goes down and does them with a free mind.
outcome: Janaka rules on as a liberated king, living in the present 'without brooding on the past or worrying about the future'.
whole_arc_note: He goes back to his duties the same day. The story is the classic case for knowledge inside action. Do not stop the telling at the roof.
teaching: A single honest moment of inquiry can free a person, who then returns to his duties without being bound by them.
framework: 1. Let what unsettles you unsettle you. 2. Take time alone. 3. Ask what in your life does not perish. 4. Resolve to look inward with reason. 5. Go back to your work.
modern_parallels: A song at a friend's funeral made me question the whole way I live.
I sat alone on my balcony after a promotion and felt nothing.
Something I heard in a podcast unsettled me for weeks.
I want to change inside without leaving my job or family.

key_verses.sanskrit: इति सिद्धगणोद्गीता गीताः श्रुत्वा महीपतिः । विषादमाजगामाशु भीरू रणरवादिव ॥
key_verses.gist: Hearing the songs sung by the siddhas, the king was suddenly dejected, like a coward at the noise of battle.

key_verses.sanskrit: परिवारमशेषेण विसृज्य स्वं स्वमालयम् । एक एवारुरोहाग्र्यं गृहमर्क इवाचलम् ॥
key_verses.gist: Sending all his household to their own rooms, he climbed alone to the highest part of the palace.

key_verses.sanskrit: शीघ्रमुत्तिष्ठ भद्रं ते नियतं कार्यमाचर । न कालमतिवर्तन्ते महान्तः स्वेषु कर्मसु ॥
key_verses.gist: Rise and do the prescribed duties; it does not become the best of men to be late in them.

content_hook: A king heard a song in his own garden and could not shake it. He climbed to his roof, alone, and by evening he was free.

title: Bhagiratha gives away everything and goes begging in the city he once ruled
the_moment: Bhagiratha is a generous and capable king, yet he is tired of it all and finds his worldly life hollow. His teacher tells him that rank and possessions sit on top of the self; he must stand where the fear of poverty and the hunger for honour cannot reach.
what_they_did: In three days he gives away all he has and hands his kingdom to his enemies. In a plain cloth he wanders, and in time comes begging to the gates of his own former city. Citizens and ministers recognise him and are grieved. The new ruler begs him to take the kingdom back. He refuses, takes only food, and walks on calmly.
the_turn: He can stand in the place of his former greatness as a beggar without shame or pride. That is the sign that his freedom is real.
outcome: Later, when a childless king dies, the people of that land make him king; his old subjects come and plead with him, and he rules both kingdoms with an even mind, and goes on to bring the Ganga down to earth.
whole_arc_note: The arc ends with him ruling again and doing the greatest work of his life. Giving everything away is his teacher's specific prescription for him and is not offered as a general rule. Do not use this to tell anyone to quit a job or give away their savings.
teaching: Freedom is tested by standing without shame where one once stood in honour; the free person can rule or beg with the same mind.
modern_parallels: I was a director and now I am unemployed in the same city where everyone knows me.
After the business failed I had to walk past my old office.
I am scared of what people will say if I take a smaller job.
Retirement took my title away and I do not know who I am without it.

key_verses.sanskrit: दिवसत्रयमात्रेण सर्वमेव परित्यजन् । असुमात्रावशेषोऽसावासीद्राजा भगीरथः ॥
key_verses.gist: In just three days he gave up everything; King Bhagiratha was left with nothing but his life.

key_verses.sanskrit: प्रभो राज्यं गृहाणेति प्रार्थितोऽप्यरिणा मुनिः । नादत्तेऽनादृताशेषस्तृणमप्यशनादृते ॥
key_verses.gist: Even when his enemy begged him, 'Lord, take back the kingdom', the sage took nothing but food.

content_hook: A king gave away his entire kingdom, then went begging at the gates of his own old capital. The people wept. He was fine.

title: Queen Chudala finds peace, and her husband laughs at her
the_moment: Chudala and Shikhidhvaja marry young and are devoted to each other. As the years pass, Chudala turns inward, inquires into the self, and comes to deep peace. Her husband notices that she looks radiant and asks what has happened. She tells him plainly: I have found the self.
dilemma: Argue to be understood, or let it be and wait.
what_they_did: He laughs out loud: 'You talk nonsense, you are just a girl. Go and enjoy your royal pleasures.' He leaves for his bath. She thinks, 'He has not understood me at all,' and returns to her duties and her inner life, saying nothing more.
the_turn: She does not need his recognition to keep what she has found. She keeps loving him, and waits for the time when he will be able to hear.
outcome: Years later, when he leaves the kingdom in despair, it is Chudala who rules in his place and finally, in disguise, becomes his teacher.
whole_arc_note: The text sides with Chudala; his laughter is shown as his blindness. Flag gender_sensitive because the dismissal is gendered and must be told as the husband's error, never as a joke. The story continues in st.yv.shikhidhvaja_burns_everything; this first part should not end on her silence as if silence were the lesson.
teaching: The truth one has found does not depend on being believed; it can wait, and keep loving.
modern_parallels: I told my husband therapy changed me and he laughed.
My family treats my spiritual practice as a phase.
At work my ideas are dismissed until a man repeats them.
I have grown and my partner still sees the person I was at twenty.

key_verses.sanskrit: असंबद्धप्रलापासि बालासि वरवर्णिनि । रमसे राजलीलाभी रमस्वावनिपात्मजे ॥
key_verses.gist: 'You babble without sense; you are just a girl, lovely one. Enjoy your royal pleasures, princess.'

key_verses.sanskrit: प्रविहस्याट्टहासेन शिखिध्वज इति प्रियाम् । मध्याह्ने स्नातुमुत्थाय निर्जगामाङ्गनागृहात् ॥
key_verses.gist: With loud laughter Shikhidhvaja rose at noon to bathe and left her rooms.

content_hook: She told her husband she had found inner peace. He laughed and called her a silly girl. Years later she became his teacher.

title: King Shikhidhvaja leaves his kingdom, burns his last possessions, and is still not free
characters: Chudala disguised as the young sage Kumbha
the_moment: Restless and unhappy, Shikhidhvaja leaves his kingdom to his wife and goes to the forest as an ascetic. Years pass. Chudala comes to him disguised as a young sage, Kumbha, and tells him he has renounced everything except the one thing that matters.
what_they_did: He piles up his hermit's belongings, his water pot, his seat, his rosary, his hut, and burns them all. 'Now I have renounced everything.' Kumbha says no. Then he says the only thing left is his body, and walks to a cliff to throw himself off. Kumbha stops him: why destroy this innocent body, which never harmed you?
the_turn: 'Neither by giving up the body, nor the kingdom, nor by burning the hut is total renunciation achieved.' What must be given up is the mind that says 'mine'.
outcome: He turns to inquire into the mind and the self, and awakens. Chudala reveals herself; they return to the kingdom and rule together, free.
whole_arc_note: SELF-HARM THEME: he moves to end his life and is stopped with the words that the body is innocent and its destruction is no renunciation. Never serve this story to a reading with any risk signal. The arc ends with return to ordinary life and rule; it is a refutation of escape, not an endorsement of it. Kumbha's test with Madanika is a later episode and can be omitted from short tellings without changing the meaning.
teaching: Renouncing things, places or even the body is not renunciation; letting go of the mind that claims them is.
modern_parallels: I quit my job, sold my stuff, moved to the mountains, and I am still miserable.
I keep changing everything outside and nothing changes inside.
I deleted every app and still feel trapped.
I thought getting away from my family would bring peace.

key_verses.sanskrit: जडो वराको मूकात्मा तपस्वी देहको ह्ययम् । न कश्चन तवैतस्मिन्मा मुधैव तनुं त्यज ॥
key_verses.gist: What is this body but dull matter that labours for you and has never harmed you? Why destroy something so innocent?

key_verses.sanskrit: साधो न देहत्यागेन न राज्यत्यजनेन च । न चोटजादिशोषेण सर्वत्यागो भवेन्नृप ॥
key_verses.gist: O king, total renunciation does not come from giving up the body, nor the kingdom, nor from burning your hut.

key_verses.sanskrit: चित्तत्यागं विदुः सर्वत्यागं त्यागविदां वर । तस्मिन्सिद्धे महाबाहो सत्यं किं नानुभूयते ॥
key_verses.gist: Renunciation is the giving up of the mind; succeed in that and you know the truth.

content_hook: He gave up his kingdom, his wife, his palace. Then he burned his last few things. His teacher said: you still have not given up the one thing that matters.

title: Kacha leaves home on his father's word, and after eight years asks why he is still not at peace
the_moment: Kacha, son of Brihaspati, is just leaving youth and asks his father how to be free. Brihaspati answers: by giving everything up. Kacha does exactly that, leaving home for the forest. His father grieves to see him go.
what_they_did: Eight years later Brihaspati finds him in the woods. Kacha says: 'Father, I have given up everything for eight years, and why do I still not have peace?' His father again says, give up all, and leaves. Kacha throws away even his bark garment and shelter, and when his father returns says, 'Now I have given up everything, and still there is no peace.'
the_turn: Brihaspati: 'When I said give up all, I meant the mind, which contains everything.' Kacha then asks what the mind is, and is taught to see it as the sense of 'I'.
outcome: Kacha inquires into the 'I', lets it go, and comes to rest.
whole_arc_note: This mirrors Shikhidhvaja's story and should not be told as a recommendation to leave home. The father's grief at his son's leaving is in the text and should stay in. The literal reading (strip yourself of possessions) is shown to fail twice before the real meaning lands.
teaching: The 'everything' that must be renounced is the mind itself, which holds all things.
modern_parallels: I did everything my guru said for years and I still do not feel free.
My son left a good job to find himself and it has been years.
I followed the advice literally and missed what it meant.
I took a sabbatical, then a longer one, and the restlessness came with me.

key_verses.sanskrit: अद्येदमष्टमं वर्षं सर्वत्यागः कृतो मया । तथापि तात विश्रान्तिं नाधिगच्छाम्यनिन्दिताम् । एवमार्तवचस्तस्मिन्कचे वदति कानने । सर्वमेव त्यजेत्युक्त्वा वाक्पतिर्दिवमुद्ययौ ॥
key_verses.gist: Father, for eight full years I have given up everything and lived alone here; why do I still not have the peace I seek?

key_verses.sanskrit: चित्तं सर्वमिति प्राहुस्तत्त्यक्त्वा पुत्र राजसे । चित्तत्यागं विदुः सर्वत्यागं सर्वविदो जनाः ॥
key_verses.gist: 'I told you to give up all, my son. That all is the mind, which contains everything.'

content_hook: His father said: give up everything. He did, for eight years. Then his father explained what he had actually meant.

title: Vasishtha asks the oldest crow in the world how he has outlived every age
the_moment: Vasishtha hears of a crow named Bhushunda who lives on a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru and has seen world-ages rise and end. He travels to meet him and asks the plain question: how have you survived, calm and unshaken, through every destruction?
what_they_did: Bhushunda answers simply. He watches the breath, the incoming and the outgoing and the pause between them. He does not brood over what he did today or worry about tomorrow. Death does not overtake one whose heart is not burned by cares.
the_turn: 'I do not fall into the fever of thoughts about past and future; that has kept me well.' Steady attention to the breath and to the present is his whole secret.
outcome: Vasishtha returns to tell the story; Bhushunda remains, serene, on his tree.
whole_arc_note: The breath practice described is detailed and meant to be learned from a teacher; use the story for the attitude (present attention, freedom from brooding) rather than as a breathing instruction. The longevity is the story's image, not a promise.
teaching: Death and fear find little hold on the one who watches the breath and is not burned by worries about past and future.
framework: 1. Watch the breath coming in and going out. 2. Notice the pause between. 3. Do not rehearse today or tomorrow. 4. Return to the breath when you drift.
modern_parallels: My anxiety is always about what I did wrong yesterday or what will go wrong tomorrow.
I want to stay calm through whatever happens in the economy.
How do people who have seen so much stay so peaceful?
I lie awake replaying the day and planning the next one.

key_verses.sanskrit: निःश्वासवृक्षक्रकचाः सर्वदेहलताघुणाः । आधयो यं न भिन्दन्ति मृत्युस्तं न जिघांसति ॥
key_verses.gist: Death does not overtake one whose body is not beset with cares like snakes, and whose heart is not burned by anxieties.

key_verses.sanskrit: किमद्य मम संपन्नं प्रातर्वा भविता पुनः । इति चिन्ताज्वरो नास्ति तेन जीवाम्यनामयः ॥
key_verses.gist: I do not think about what I did today or must do tomorrow, nor suffer the fever of thoughts of past and future; this has kept me well.

content_hook: A sage asked a crow that had lived through every end of the world how he stayed so calm. The crow's answer was about breathing.

title: The fruit of immortality that came back to the king
source_ref: Legend, not text: frame-story of the Vikrama-charita (Simhasana-dvatrimshika, unit II; Edgerton 1926); the verse the king speaks is Niti Shataka 2 (popular numbering)
the_moment: A poor brahmin is given a fruit that grants long life. Thinking a long life of poverty useless, he gives it to the king. The king, deeply in love, gives it to his queen. Days later the same fruit is placed back in his hands by someone else. He traces it: it has passed from the queen to someone she loved, and from that person onwards, until it came back to him.
what_they_did: In the legend he speaks one verse that curses no one alone: 'She of whom I always think is indifferent to me; she wants another, who is attached to someone else, while yet another pines for me. Fie on her, on him, on Love, on that one, and on me.' He gives the throne to his brother Vikrama and leaves.
the_turn: He includes himself in the verdict ('and on me'). The chain shows him that every one of them, himself first, was chasing someone who was chasing someone else.
outcome: He becomes a renunciant; the tradition holds that he then wrote the Vairagya Shataka.
whole_arc_note: LEGEND, NOT TEXT. Mark it as tradition every time. The source framing contains generalisations against women; leave them all out (rule: content that demeans women stays out) and never single out the queen as the villain or describe any punishment of her (a variant has her executed; do not use). Keep the focus on the king's attachment and his own 'and on me'. Scholars doubt that the poet was a king (Wortham, Kosambi).
teaching: Attachment runs in a chain where each chases someone who chases another; seeing the chain, including oneself in it, frees.
modern_parallels: I found out the gift I gave her was passed on to someone else.
I love someone who loves someone who does not love them back.
The betrayal hurt, but what hurt more was seeing how blind I had been.
I keep chasing approval from people who are chasing someone else's.

key_verses.sanskrit: यां चिन्तयामि सततं मयि सा विरक्ता साप्यन्यमिच्छति जनं स जनोऽन्यसक्तः । अस्मत्कृते च परिशुष्यति काचिदन्या धिक् तां च तं च मदनं च इमां च मां च ॥
key_verses.gist: She I think of always is indifferent to me; she desires another; he is attached to someone else; another woman pines for me. Fie on her, on him, on Love, on that woman, and on me.

key_verses.sanskrit: अवश्यं यातारश्चिरतरमुषित्वापि विषया वियोगे को भेदस्त्यजति न जनो यत्स्वयममून् । व्रजन्तः स्वातन्त्र्यादतुलपरितापाय मनसः स्वयं त्यक्ता ह्येते शमसुखमनन्तं विदधति ॥
key_verses.gist: Objects of sense must leave us one day; if they leave us we suffer, if we let them go ourselves we gain endless peace.

content_hook: A king gave a magic fruit to the woman he loved. A few days later someone else handed it back to him. The verse he spoke next is still recited.

title: 'I swallowed my tears and laughed with an empty heart'
the_moment: The poet looks back on years of chasing favour. He has put up with the talk of crude men to keep them pleased. He has held back his tears and laughed at their jokes with an empty heart. He has folded his hands before people whose minds were stiff with money.
what_they_did: He turns and speaks to his own hope directly: 'O Hope, you useless hope, what more will you make me dance to?'
the_turn: He sees that the people were never the master; his own hope was, and it made him dance.
outcome: The verse sits among others in which the poet slowly loosens craving's grip.
whole_arc_note: The verse is a confession, not advice to quit a job. Its force is in naming who held the strings. Pair with a verse on self-respect (Niti 31) or contentment, never with a verse that blames the reader.
teaching: It is our own hope of gain that makes us flatter and smile on cue; seeing that is the start of dignity.
modern_parallels: I laugh at my boss's jokes and hate myself on the drive home.
I have spent years pleasing clients who do not respect me.
I smile in meetings while something in me is crying.
I keep hoping the next promotion will make all this worth it.

key_verses.sanskrit: खलालापाः सोढाः कथमपि तदाराधनपरैः निगृह्यान्तर्बाष्पं हसितमपि शून्येन मनसा । कृतो वित्तस्तम्भप्रतिहतधियामञ्जलिरपि त्वमाशे मोघाशे किमपरमतो नर्तयसि माम् ॥
key_verses.gist: I bore the talk of the wicked to please them, held back tears and laughed with an empty mind, bowed to fools stiff with money. O Hope, what more will you make me dance to?

content_hook: Fifteen hundred years ago a poet wrote about laughing at his boss's jokes while holding back tears. Then he named who was really in charge.

title: Grey hair, wrinkled face, weak limbs, and craving alone stays young
the_moment: He looks at himself honestly. His face is lined, his head is white, his limbs grow slack. Friends his age have died. He walks with a stick. And the wanting in him is as young as ever.
what_they_did: He puts it in four lines: 'We did not enjoy pleasures; we were enjoyed. We did not do penance; we were burned. Time did not pass; we passed. Craving did not grow old; we grew old.'
the_turn: The reversal in each line: what he thought he was doing was being done to him.
outcome: The verses lead into the poet's turn towards the lasting.
whole_arc_note: Never use this to mock ageing or the body. Its point is the mismatch between an ageing life and an unaged wanting. Light enough for a reel, deep enough for week 2.
teaching: We think we consume pleasures, but they consume us; time does not pass, we do, and craving never ages.
modern_parallels: I am fifty-five and still checking stock prices every hour.
My body is tired but I still want more of everything.
I thought the wanting would calm down with age. It has not.
I spent my youth chasing things and now I see they were chasing me.

key_verses.sanskrit: भोगा न भुक्ता वयमेव भुक्ताः तपो न तप्तं वयमेव तप्ताः । कालो न यातो वयमेव याता- स्तृष्णा न जीर्णा वयमेव जीर्णाः ॥
key_verses.gist: Pleasures were not enjoyed; we were enjoyed. Penance was not done; we were burned. Time did not go; we went. Craving did not age; we aged.

key_verses.sanskrit: वलीभिर्मुखमाक्रान्तं पलितेनाङ्कितं शिरः । गात्राणि शिथिलायन्ते तृष्णैका तरुणायते ॥
key_verses.gist: My face is lined, my head is grey, my limbs are slack; only craving grows young.

content_hook: 'Time did not pass. We did.' A king-poet wrote four lines about ageing that hit harder every year.

title: A proud man stammers a request, only because his children are hungry
the_moment: A man of pride would never ask anyone for anything for himself. But he sees his wife in a worn sari, with hungry children tugging at it and crying, and nothing in the house.
dilemma: Keep his pride, or ask and risk refusal.
what_they_did: He asks. His throat tightens, his words break and fade with the fear of refusal, but he says 'give'.
the_turn: The verse holds both: asking is agony to him, and for them he does it.
outcome: The verse does not say whether he was given anything.
whole_arc_note: Bhartrihari's section condemns begging for one's own wants, and this verse marks the exception: asking for those who depend on you. Do not use it to shame anyone who asks for help; the verse honours the man who asks.
teaching: A self-respecting person will not beg for himself, but will swallow his pride for those who depend on him.
modern_parallels: I lost my job and had to ask my brother-in-law for money for the kids' fees.
I would rather starve than ask, but my daughter needs her medicine.
I called my old boss for a favour and my voice shook.
I have never asked anyone for anything and now I have to.

key_verses.sanskrit: दीना दीनमुखैः सदैव शिशुकैराकृष्टजीर्णाम्बरा क्रोशद्भिः क्षुधितैर्निरन्नविधुरा दृश्या न चेद्गेहिनी । याञ्चाभङ्गभयेन गद्गदगलत्त्रुट्यद्विलीनाक्षरं को देहीति वदेत्स्वदग्धजठरस्यार्थे मनस्वी पुमान् ॥
key_verses.gist: If he did not see his wife, worn sari pulled by crying hungry children, what proud man would say 'give', his voice breaking for fear of refusal, for his own belly's sake?

content_hook: He would never ask anyone for anything. Then he saw his children hungry. A 1,500-year-old verse about the hardest word a father says.

title: Those who never start, those who quit at the first wall, and those who keep going
the_moment: The verse draws three people standing before the same task. The first does not begin, afraid of what might go wrong. The second begins and stops when the first obstacle hits. The third is struck by obstacles again and again.
what_they_did: The third does not let go of what was begun.
the_turn: 'Prarabdham uttamajana na parityajanti': the best do not abandon what they have started, however often they are struck down.
whole_arc_note: Wortham reads it of the pursuit of wisdom; it is usually applied to any worthy undertaking. Do not use it to shame someone who stopped for good reason (illness, harm); it is about stopping out of fear.
teaching: The lowly do not start for fear of obstacles; the middling stop when obstacles come; the best never give up what they have begun.
framework: 1. Notice which of the three you are today. 2. If you have not started, start small. 3. When the wall comes, expect it. 4. Count how many times you have been struck and are still going.
modern_parallels: I have had the idea for my startup for three years and never begun.
I start every diet and quit on day four.
My side project has failed twice and I am deciding whether to try again.
I want to be the kind of person who finishes.

key_verses.sanskrit: प्रारभ्यते न खलु विघ्नभयेन नीचैः प्रारभ्य विघ्नविहता विरमन्ति मध्याः ॥ विघ्नैः पुनः पुनरपि प्रतिहन्यमानाः प्रारब्धमुत्तमगुणा न परित्यजन्ति ॥
key_verses.gist: The low do not begin for fear of obstacles; the middling begin and stop when obstacles strike; the best, struck again and again, do not abandon what they began.

content_hook: There are three kinds of people, a poet wrote. The ones who never start. The ones who stop at the first wall. And the third kind.

title: An ascetic in bark faces a king in silk: who is the poor one?
the_moment: An ascetic stands before a king who takes no notice of him. The king is famous for his riches; the ascetic for his learning, praised by poets. The king commands wealth; the ascetic, words. If the king does not care for him, he does not care for the king either.
what_they_did: He says: 'We are content here in bark, you in silk. The contentment is the same; there is no difference. He is poor whose craving is vast. When the mind is content, who is rich and who is poor?'
the_turn: He moves the measure from what one has to how much one wants.
whole_arc_note: Some verses in this section praise living on alms and are monastic in tone; the usable centre is verse 53 on contentment. Do not use it to tell a person in real poverty that their need is only in the mind.
teaching: The poor one is whoever has vast craving; where the mind is content, rich and poor are the same.
modern_parallels: My college friend is a CEO and I am a schoolteacher, and I feel small at reunions.
Everyone in my building has a bigger car.
Am I poor, or do I just want too much?
I am content most days until I open Instagram.

key_verses.sanskrit: त्वं राजा वयमप्युपासितगुरुप्रज्ञाभिमानोन्नताः ख्यातस्त्वं विभवैर्यशांसि कवयो दिक्षु प्रतन्वन्ति नः । इत्थं मानधनातिदूरमुभयोरप्यावयोरन्तरं यद्यस्मासु पराङ्मुखोऽसि वयमप्येकान्ततो निःस्पृहाः ॥
key_verses.gist: You are a king; we too are honoured for wisdom. You are famed for riches; poets spread our fame.

key_verses.sanskrit: वयमिह परितुष्टा वल्कलैस्त्वं दुकूलैः सम इव परितोषो निर्विशेषो विशेषः । स तु भवतु दरिद्रो यस्य तृष्णा विशाला मनसि च परितुष्टे कोऽर्थवान्को दरिद्रः ॥
key_verses.gist: We are content in bark, you in silk; the contentment is equal. He is poor whose craving is vast; when the mind is content, who is rich and who is poor?

content_hook: A man in tree bark stood before a king in silk and asked one question: which of us is poor?

title: The house where there were many, and now there is one
the_moment: He looks at a house. Where once there were many, now there is one. Where there was one, then there were many, and at the end not even one. The people who gave him birth left long ago; those he grew up with are only memories.
what_they_did: He watches time toss the days and nights like dice, and sees himself 'day by day nearing the fall, like trees on a sandy riverbank'.
the_turn: Naming it without flinching: this is what time does to every house.
outcome: The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
whole_arc_note: These are elegy verses. They name loss and do not prescribe; never follow them in a plan with a verse that tells a griever to stop grieving. Good as a see_name day for empty nest, ageing parents, or a family home sold.
teaching: Time empties houses one by one; those who bore us and those we grew with become memories, and we are next.
modern_parallels: Our ancestral house had twenty people at Diwali; now it is just my mother.
My kids left for college and the house is so quiet.
My parents are gone and my school friends are only in WhatsApp groups.
We are selling the family home and I keep walking through the empty rooms.

key_verses.sanskrit: यत्रानेकः क्वचिदपि गृहे तत्र तिष्ठत्यथैको यत्राप्येकस्तदनु बहवस्तत्र नैकोऽपि चान्ते । इत्थं नेयौ रजनिदिवसौ लोलयन्द्वाविवाक्षौ कालः कल्यो भुवनफलके क्रीडति प्राणिशारैः ॥
key_verses.gist: In the house where there were many, now there is one; where there was one, there were many, and at last not even one.

key_verses.sanskrit: वयं येभ्यो जाताश्चिरपरिचिता एव खलु ते समं यैः संवृद्धाः स्मृतिविषयतां तेऽपि गमिताः । इदानीमेते स्मः प्रतिदिवसमासन्नपतना गतास्तुल्यावस्थां सिकतिलनदीतीरतरुभिः ॥
key_verses.gist: Those who bore us have long gone; those we grew up with are memories; we too are near the fall, like trees on a sandy bank.

content_hook: 'In the house where there were many, now there is one.' A line from 1,500 years ago that describes every family home.

title: The dog rolls over for the hand that feeds it; the elephant waits to be coaxed
the_moment: Two scenes. A dog finds a dry bone with a scrap of fat on it and is overjoyed, though it does nothing for its hunger. Before the man who gives it food, the dog wags its tail, falls at his feet, rolls on the ground and shows its belly. The great elephant looks on steadily and eats only when coaxed with a hundred kind words.
what_they_did: The lion, the poet adds, passes over the jackal at its feet and goes for the elephant.
the_turn: Dignity is in how one receives, not in what one receives.
whole_arc_note: The library notes some verses in this section lean towards intolerance of insult (a warrior-king ideal). Use these two for self-respect, not for pride or for contempt of people who must ask for work or help.
teaching: The small-minded grovel for scraps; the great receive with steadiness and self-respect.
modern_parallels: I say yes to every client demand because I am scared to lose them.
I am so grateful for any attention from my manager that I embarrass myself.
I want to stop chasing people who throw me scraps.
I accepted a lowball offer because I felt I should be thankful.

key_verses.sanskrit: स्वल्पस्नायुवसावशेषमलिनं निर्मांसमप्यस्थिकं श्वा लब्ध्वा परितोषमेति न तु तत्तस्य क्षुधाशान्तये । सिंहो जम्बुकमङ्कमागतमपि त्यक्त्वा निहन्ति द्विपं सर्वः कृच्छ्रगतोऽपि वाञ्छति जनः सत्वानुरुपं फलम् ॥
key_verses.gist: A dog delights in a filthy fleshless bone that will not ease its hunger; a lion passes the jackal by and kills the elephant.

key_verses.sanskrit: लाङ्गूलचालनमधश्चरणावपातं भूमौ निपत्य वदनोदरदर्शनं च । श्वा पिण्डदस्य कुरुते गजपुङ्गवस्तु धीरं विलोकयति चाटुशतैश्च भुङ्क्ते ॥
key_verses.gist: The dog wags its tail, falls at the feet, rolls over and shows its belly to the one who feeds it; the great elephant looks on steadily and eats only when coaxed.

content_hook: A dog rolls over for anyone holding food. An elephant waits. A 1,500-year-old verse about how you take what you are given.

title: Chased by monkeys in Varanasi, he hears a stranger shout 'Face the brutes'
source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'What Is Religion?', Complete Works vol. 1 (his own account)
the_moment: In Varanasi he is walking a narrow way with a tank of water on one side and a high wall on the other. A troop of big, surly monkeys decide not to let him pass. They shriek, clutch at his feet and press closer. He starts to run, and the faster he runs, the faster they come, biting at him.
what_they_did: A stranger calls out to him: 'Face the brutes.' He turns and faces the monkeys. They fall back and finally run away.
the_turn: Turning round. 'Like the monkeys, the hardships of life fall back when we cease to flee before them.'
outcome: He draws the lesson for all life: face the terrible, face it boldly.
whole_arc_note: Documented in his own words in a lecture. The common retelling names the stranger as an old sannyasi; the CW text says only 'a stranger'. Do not use it for a situation of real physical danger or abuse, where safety comes first and 'face it' could harm; it speaks to fears and troubles one has been running from.
teaching: The troubles we flee from chase us; when we turn and face them, they fall back.
framework: 1. Notice what you are running from. 2. Notice that running makes it chase harder. 3. Stop. 4. Turn and look at it squarely.
modern_parallels: I have been avoiding opening my credit card statements for months.
The more I avoid the conversation with my father, the bigger it gets.
I run from every difficult email and they pile up.
My anxiety gets worse every time I cancel plans to avoid it.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 1, WHAT IS RELIGION?
key_verses.quote: I met a stranger who called out to me, "Face the brutes." I turned and faced the monkeys, and they fell back and finally fled. That is a lesson for all life
key_verses.gist: He ran, the monkeys came faster; a stranger cried, Face the brutes; he turned and they fled.

content_hook: Monkeys chased Vivekananda down a lane in Varanasi. The faster he ran, the faster they came. Then a stranger shouted three words.

title: The frog in the well meets a frog from the sea
source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'Why We Disagree', Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 15 September 1893, Complete Works vol. 1
the_moment: A frog has lived all its life in a well, born there and grown sleek there, keeping it clean. One day a frog from the sea falls in. 'Where are you from?' 'From the sea.' 'The sea! How big is that? Is it as big as my well?' And it leaps from one side of the well to the other.
what_they_did: The sea frog says there is no comparison. The well frog leaps again: 'Is your sea so big?' Finally: 'Nothing can be bigger than my well. This fellow is a liar; turn him out.'
the_turn: Vivekananda turns it on his audience: each of us sits in a little well and thinks the whole world is that well.
outcome: He ends by thanking America for trying to break down the barriers of the little worlds.
whole_arc_note: He told it to explain why religions quarrel, and included the Hindu in the well too. Use it against narrowness of any kind, never to mock a particular faith or person.
teaching: Each of us sits in a small well and calls it the whole world; the wider truth seems a lie from inside the well.
modern_parallels: I grew up in a small town and dismissed everything I had not seen.
My father thinks his way is the only way to run a business.
I argued that my religion was the only true one and then I met people who changed my mind.
Moving abroad showed me how small my world was.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 1, WHY WE DISAGREE
key_verses.quote: A frog lived in a well. It had lived there for a long time.
key_verses.gist: A frog lived in a well; one day a frog from the sea fell in.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 1, WHY WE DISAGREE
key_verses.quote: nothing can be bigger than my well
key_verses.gist: Nothing can be bigger than my well; this fellow is a liar, turn him out.

content_hook: 'Is the sea as big as my well?' Vivekananda told this story in Chicago in 1893, and the audience was the frog.

title: A lion cub raised by sheep, who bleats and runs
source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'The Real Nature of Man', Complete Works vol. 2 (also vols 1, 3, 7)
the_moment: A lioness dies leaping on a flock of sheep and gives birth as she falls. The cub is raised by the sheep. It eats grass and bleats. Grown huge, it still thinks it is a sheep and runs with the flock when danger comes.
what_they_did: Another lion sees it and is astonished. It tries to approach, but the sheep-lion flees. It waits, finds it asleep, and says, 'You are a lion.' 'I am a sheep,' it cries, and bleats. The lion drags it to a lake: 'Look, here is my reflection and yours.'
the_turn: It looks at the lion, then at its own reflection, and in a moment knows it is a lion. It roars, and the bleating is gone.
outcome: 'You are lions, you are souls, pure, infinite and perfect.'
whole_arc_note: He uses it for the Vedantic claim that weakness is a mistaken identity, not a sin. Use it for self-worth and the self level; do not use it to tell a struggling person they are simply choosing to be weak.
teaching: We are not weak or sinful by nature; we have forgotten what we are, and one clear look can show it.
modern_parallels: I grew up being told I was not smart and I still believe it.
Everyone in my family plays safe and so I run from every risk.
I keep shrinking in a room full of people who are less capable than me.
A mentor once showed me who I could be and I did not believe them.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 2, THE REAL NATURE OF MAN
key_verses.quote: You are lions, you are souls, pure, infinite, and perfect.
key_verses.gist: The lion dragged him to a lake; he saw his reflection, knew he was a lion, roared.

content_hook: A lion raised by sheep ate grass and bleated its whole life. Then another lion dragged it to a lake.

title: A young man asks every preacher in Calcutta, 'Have you seen God?'
source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'The Vedanta in All Its Phases' (Calcutta, 1897), Complete Works vol. 3 (his own account)
the_moment: As a boy in Calcutta he goes from lecture to lecture in search of religion. He hears big talks. Afterwards he goes up to each speaker with one question: 'Have you seen God?'
what_they_did: Each speaker is taken aback by the idea of seeing God. He keeps asking.
the_turn: 'The only man who told me, "I have", was Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, and not only so, but he said, "I will put you in the way of seeing Him too."'
outcome: He becomes Ramakrishna's disciple; he later says a guru is one who knows the meaning, not one who twists texts.
whole_arc_note: Documented in his own words. Popular retellings add Ramakrishna's further words ('as I see you, only more intensely'); those are from the Gospel and biographies, not this lecture, and should be marked if used. His honest doubt was the qualification, not an obstacle.
teaching: Religion is realisation; ask for the one who has seen, and keep asking until you find them.
modern_parallels: I have heard a hundred sermons and I just want to know if anyone actually knows.
I left my faith because nobody could answer my questions honestly.
I want a teacher who has lived it, not one who has read it.
My doubts feel like a sin, but they are the most honest thing about me.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 3, THE VEDANTA IN ALL ITS PHASES
key_verses.quote: everywhere I asked the lecturer after hearing very big lectures, "Have you seen God?"
key_verses.gist: Everywhere I asked, Have you seen God? The only man who said I have was Ramakrishna.

content_hook: As a teenager he asked every famous preacher in Calcutta one question. Only one man said yes.

title: His father dies, the family is starving, and he is torn between them and his calling
source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'My Life and Mission' (Pasadena, 1900), Complete Works vol. 8 (his own account)
the_moment: Ramakrishna has died. The dozen boys around him are laughed at, then persecuted; their own parents are furious. At the same time his father dies and the family is left 'very poor, almost starving all the time'. He is the only one who can help them.
dilemma: See his mother and brothers suffer, or abandon the work he believes is for the good of India and the world.
what_they_did: 'The fight went on in my mind for days and months.' He prays for five or six days and nights at a time. 'Oh, the agony of those days! I was living in hell!' The one person who sympathises is Ramakrishna's widow, poorer than they are.
the_turn: He decides the ideas must not die and plunges in, knowing the cost.
outcome: He goes on to wander India and then to Chicago. (From the biographies, not this text: the Raja of Khetri later sent a monthly allowance to his mother.)
whole_arc_note: Told in his own words, with its harshest line ('What if a mother or two brothers die? It is a sacrifice'). Do not quote that line as advice; it is a man describing his own agony. NOT for anyone being pushed to abandon dependents, a caregiver, or a parent of young children. Use it to honour how hard a calling against family duty is, not to settle such a choice for anyone.
teaching: Great work is rarely done without a terrible inner struggle between love for one's own and the call one believes in.
modern_parallels: My father died and I am the only earner, and I had just started my own company.
My family needs me to take a safe job and I feel called to something else.
I am torn between staying for my parents and leaving for my dream.
Nobody around me understands what I am trying to build.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 8, MY LIFE AND MISSION
key_verses.quote: I had to stand between my two worlds.
key_verses.gist: My father died; we were left almost starving; I was the only hope of the family; the fight went on in my mind for days and months.

content_hook: His father died, his family was starving, and everyone mocked the work he believed in. In his own words: I was living in hell.

title: 'I was not good enough to that person': a letter to a grieving friend
source_ref: Letter to Mary Hale, Pasadena, 20 February 1900, Complete Works vol. 8
the_moment: Mary Hale writes to tell him her father has died. It is her first grief of this kind. Her mother and sister are in sorrow too.
what_they_did: He writes back that in spite of monastic training, 'the heart lives on'. Then he tells her something about himself: 'The most curious cause of suffering when somebody goes off is the feeling that I was not good enough to that person. When my father died, it was a pang for months, and I had been so disobedient.'
the_turn: He names the guilt that comes with grief and loosens it gently: 'You have been very dutiful; if you feel anything like that, it is only a form of sorrow.'
outcome: He adds that experience is the one teacher; 'through smiles and tears we learn'.
whole_arc_note: Documented letter. Its gift is that a great teacher admits his own regret about his father. Safe for griever plans; does not tell anyone to stop grieving.
teaching: The feeling that we were not good enough to the one we lost is itself a form of sorrow, not a verdict.
modern_parallels: Since my father died I keep thinking of every time I snapped at him.
I was not there enough in her last year, and I cannot forgive myself.
Everyone says I was a good daughter but I do not feel it.
I fought with my mother the week before she died.

key_verses.quote: the most curious cause of suffering when somebody goes off is the feeling that I was not good enough to that person.
key_verses.gist: The most curious cause of suffering when somebody goes is the feeling I was not good enough to that person; when my father died it was a pang for months.

content_hook: When a friend's father died, Vivekananda wrote to her about his own father, and the guilt nobody talks about.

title: A proud young ascetic is taught by a housewife and a butcher
source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'What Is Duty?' (Karma-Yoga ch. 4), Complete Works vol. 1; retelling of the Vyadha Gita, Mahabharata, Vana Parva
the_moment: After years of practice in the forest, a young ascetic is sitting under a tree when dry leaves fall on his head. A crow and a crane are fighting above. In anger he glares at them and a flash of fire burns them to ashes. He is delighted with his power.
what_they_did: He goes to town to beg and a woman calls, 'Wait a little, my son.' He fumes: 'You do not know my power.' She calls again: 'Boy, don't be thinking too much of yourself. Here is neither crow nor crane.' She was nursing her sick husband; doing her duty all her life is her only yoga. She sends him to a butcher in the market. The butcher finishes his work, takes him home, washes and feeds his old parents, and only then sits to teach him.
the_turn: The ordinary duty done whole-heartedly is shown to be higher than the powers he had prized.
outcome: The Vyadha's teaching becomes the Vyadha Gita; the young man learns that no duty is low.
whole_arc_note: The source has a translator's footnote describing the Vyadha's caste in demeaning terms; leave it out. The point of the story is that the hierarchy of station is overturned. The woman is the first teacher and is illumined; do not reduce her to a model of wifely service. Flag gender_sensitive for that reason.
teaching: Doing the duty in front of you, wholeheartedly and without attachment, leads higher than any special power.
modern_parallels: I thought my meditation made me better than my family, and then my mother read me like a book.
I look down on my 'boring' job but the person who does it well is calmer than me.
I got angry when someone made me wait, and later found out why.
My spiritual practice has made me more arrogant, not less.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 1, WHAT IS DUTY?
key_verses.quote: "Boy, don't be thinking too much of yourself. Here is neither crow nor crane."
key_verses.gist: 'Boy, do not think too much of yourself. Here is neither crow nor crane.'

content_hook: A yogi burned two birds with a glance. Then a woman at a doorway told him exactly what he had done, and sent him to a butcher for lessons.

title: A man gets a ghost that must be kept busy, or it will eat him
source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'We Help Ourselves, Not the World' (Karma-Yoga ch. 5), Complete Works vol. 1
characters: a dog with a curly tail
the_moment: A poor man hears that a ghost will do anything you command, and pesters a sage until he gives him the charm. The sage warns him: ghosts must be kept busy every moment, or they will take your life. 'That is easy,' says the man.
what_they_did: The ghost builds a palace, brings money, clears a forest and builds a city, each in a moment. 'Anything more?' The man runs out of tasks and the ghost moves to eat him. He runs back to the sage, who tells him to cut off the curly tail of a dog and give it to the ghost to straighten.
the_turn: The ghost straightens the tail; let go, it curls up again; and again. The ghost gives up and asks to be released.
outcome: Vivekananda says the world is like the dog's curly tail; people have tried to straighten it for hundreds of years. Know that, and work without fanaticism and without expecting the world to become perfect.
whole_arc_note: Told with humour. Its point, in context, is that we help ourselves by doing good, the world will not be finally fixed, and a restless mind that must always be fed is a danger. Do not use it to say that effort to improve things is pointless; the chapter urges work, without fanaticism.
teaching: The world, like a curly tail, will not be made straight for good; work for it anyway, and do not let the restless mind devour you.
modern_parallels: I cannot sit still; if I have no task I feel like I am disappearing.
I keep trying to fix my relative and he goes back to the same habits.
I finish my to-do list and immediately feel panic.
I wanted success badly, got it, and now it demands everything.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 1, WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD
key_verses.quote: they are terrible beings, and must be kept continually busy.
key_verses.gist: Ghosts must be kept constantly busy; fail to give him work and he will take your life.

content_hook: A man got a ghost that could do any job in a second, and would eat him the moment he ran out of jobs. Sound familiar?

title: Seven thousand people, every speaker prepared, and he has nothing written
source_ref: Letter to Alasinga Perumal, Chicago, 2 November 1893, Complete Works vol. 5 (his own account)
the_moment: He has just come through a stretch of having no money and no one in America who knew him. On the opening morning of the Parliament he sits on a platform before six or seven thousand people. He has never spoken in public. The other delegates have ready-made speeches and are applauded.
what_they_did: 'My heart was fluttering, and my tongue nearly dried up; I was so nervous and could not venture to speak in the morning.' He lets his turn pass. Later he bows to Devi Saraswati, steps up, and begins: 'Sisters and Brothers of America'.
the_turn: A small act of surrender before stepping up, after admitting to himself that he had nothing prepared.
outcome: 'A deafening applause of two minutes followed.' Within weeks he writes that he is out of want and many doors are open to him.
whole_arc_note: Documented in his own letter, which is honest about nerves and about having been 'out of pocket' just before. Keep the fear in; the story is about walking up while afraid, not about being naturally fearless.
teaching: One can be unprepared and terrified and still step up, after a moment of surrender.
framework: 1. Admit the fear. 2. Let the moment pass if you must, but do not leave. 3. Make a small act of surrender. 4. Stand up and begin with what is true.
modern_parallels: I have my first big presentation tomorrow and everyone else is more polished than me.
I skipped my turn to speak in the meeting because my throat went dry.
I am the only one here who does not belong.
I moved to a new country with no network and I am down to my last savings.

key_verses.quote: Of course my heart was fluttering, and my tongue nearly dried up
key_verses.gist: My heart was fluttering, my tongue nearly dried up; I could not venture to speak in the morning; I had no speech; I bowed to Saraswati and stepped up.

content_hook: Before 'Sisters and Brothers of America', Vivekananda was so nervous he let his turn pass all morning. He wrote about it to a friend.

title: A sage who would not answer questions, and then said: 'Let the end and the means be joined'
source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'What Is Duty?' (Karma-Yoga ch. 4), Complete Works vol. 1; the sage is identified in the tradition as Pavhari Baba (from memory, not stated here)
characters: a yogi of Ghazipur (Pavhari Baba, per tradition)
the_moment: He meets a yogi he calls one of the most wonderful men he has ever seen. The man will not take the role of a teacher; asked a question, he says nothing.
what_they_did: He learns to ask and then wait. Days later, in the middle of ordinary conversation, the sage brings the subject up himself and throws light on it.
the_turn: The secret of work, the sage told him once: 'Let the end and the means be joined into one.' When doing any work, do not think of anything beyond it; do it as worship.
outcome: Vivekananda makes it the key to the whole Vyadha story: the housewife and the butcher became illumined by doing their duty wholeheartedly, without attachment to results.
whole_arc_note: The identification with Pavhari Baba comes from Vivekananda's other writings and biographies, not this passage; mark it. Do not present the waiting as a technique to extract answers; it is respect for a teacher's way.
teaching: When the means and the end become one, work done wholly in the present becomes worship and frees us from worry over results.
framework: 1. Pick the one task in front of you. 2. Do not think beyond it while doing it. 3. Treat it as worship. 4. Let the result come in its own time.
modern_parallels: I cannot enjoy my work because I am always thinking about the appraisal.
I keep checking whether my post went viral instead of writing the next one.
I want to stop living for the outcome and start living in the doing.
I asked my mentor a question and the answer came weeks later in a different conversation.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 1, WHAT IS DUTY?
key_verses.quote: "Let the end and the means be joined into one."
key_verses.gist: He told me once the secret of work: 'Let the end and the means be joined into one.'

content_hook: He met a yogi who refused to answer questions. Days later the yogi said six words that became Vivekananda's secret of work.

title: An old friend from home tells America he is a fraud
source_ref: Letters to Alasinga Perumal (1894) and to Professor J. H. Wright (1894), Complete Works vols 5 and 7 (his own words)
the_moment: After Chicago, some clergymen attack him. Then the blow that hurts: Mazoomdar, a respected man from Calcutta whom he counted an old friend, tells people in America he is a fraud and a rogue, and in Calcutta says he is living an unchaste life.
dilemma: Defend himself publicly, or let it go and keep working.
what_they_did: He writes privately to friends how it shocked him: 'the fever of jealousy which attacked Mazoomdar gave me a terrible shock'. To the professor who had vouched for him he gives every assurance, but asks him not to publish anything: 'the Sannyasin must not have self-defence'. Of Mazoomdar he writes, 'Lord bless him!' and 'he is a great and good man who has tried all his life to do good'.
the_turn: He separates the hurt from the man. He names the jealousy, prays the man will know better, and keeps his attention on the work: 'no good thing can be done without obstruction'.
outcome: The work goes on; he later notes that one of the papers praising him is edited by Mazoomdar's own cousin, and that 'he has injured his cause by telling lies through jealousy. Lord knows I never attempted any defence.'
whole_arc_note: Keep the hurt in: he calls it a terrible shock and is not serene at first. His refusal to defend himself is tied to his monastic vow; do not present it as what every wronged person should do. A wronged user may need to defend their name; this story shows how to keep the heart free of hatred while the facts are handled.
teaching: When someone you trusted slanders you out of jealousy, you can name the hurt, refuse to hate, and let the work answer.
framework: 1. Admit the shock to someone you trust. 2. Give the people who matter the facts privately. 3. Name the other person's jealousy without hating them. 4. Return to the work.
modern_parallels: A colleague I helped is spreading lies about me to the leadership.
Someone from my own community is badmouthing me now that I am doing well.
My oldest friend told people I am a fraud.
I want to post a long reply defending myself and I do not know if I should.

key_verses.quote: He has told them that I was a big fraud, and a rogue!
key_verses.gist: Mazoomdar has told them I was a big fraud and a rogue. Lord bless him! No good thing can be done without obstruction.

key_verses.quote: the Sannyasin must not have self-defence
key_verses.gist: The fever of jealousy which attacked Mazoomdar gave me a terrible shock, and I pray he would know better.

content_hook: After his triumph in Chicago, an old friend from home told America that Vivekananda was a fraud. Here is what he wrote about it in private.

title: A poor widow's small son is afraid to walk home through the woods
source_ref: Swami Vivekananda, 'The Story of the Boy Gopala', Complete Works vol. 6 (a devotional tale he retold)
the_moment: Gopala's mother is a widow, very poor, who has toiled at her spinning wheel for months to buy his school things. One winter afternoon he tells her he is afraid to walk home alone through the dark woods; other boys have someone to fetch them. 'Never before had she felt her widowhood, her loneliness, her poverty so bitter.'
what_they_did: For a moment it is all dark; then she remembers the promise that the Lord carries what is needed for those who depend on him. She wipes her tears and tells her son that another son of hers, also called Gopala, tends cattle in the wood; if he is afraid he has only to call his brother.
the_turn: The child believes his mother, calls, and a voice answers from the trees: 'Don't be afraid, little brother, I am here.' Later, when the other boys sneer because he has no gift for the teacher, the cowherd gives him a small pot of cream that will not empty.
outcome: The mother, hearing of it day by day, forgets her poverty and blesses her hardships. When the teacher demands to see the cowherd, only a voice comes: 'Thy mother's and thy love and faith brought Me to thee; tell thy teacher he will have to wait a long while yet.'
whole_arc_note: This is a devotional tale Vivekananda retold, not history; say so. The text describes the widow as waiting for death to rejoin her husband; that line should not be presented as an ideal for widows. The miracle answers the faith of mother and child; do not use it to promise that a frightened parent's child will be magically protected. Use it for a parent's loneliness and the trust she passes on.
teaching: A parent's faith, passed to a child, makes the child unafraid; love and faith, more than learning, bring the Lord near.
modern_parallels: I am a single mother and my son is scared to take the school bus alone.
Other kids' parents can afford things I cannot, and my daughter notices.
I feel my loneliness most when my child needs something I cannot give.
I want to give my child faith, not just fear.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 6, THE STORY OF THE BOY GOPALA
key_verses.quote: Never before had she felt her widowhood, her loneliness, her poverty so bitter.
key_verses.gist: Never before had she felt her widowhood, loneliness and poverty so bitter; then she recalled the promise.

key_verses.ref: Complete Works vol 6, THE STORY OF THE BOY GOPALA
key_verses.quote: "Don't be afraid, little brother, I am here; go home without fear."
key_verses.gist: Don't be afraid, little brother, I am here; go home without fear.

content_hook: A small boy was scared to walk home through the woods. His mother had no one to send with him. So she told him he had a brother in the forest.
